angle: What are we really looking at in the most famous gap in art?
answer: A sculptor's painting made standing in pain on a scaffold, showing the instant before life passes from God to a still-limp Adam; part of Adam's hand was repainted in the 1560s after the plaster cracked, a 1990 theory reads God's cloak as a human brain, and the colours we see were only uncovered by the 1980s-90s cleaning.
logline: Part of Adam's famous finger isn't Michelangelo's, so what are we looking at? A pope ordered a sculptor to paint a ceiling, but he didn't lie on his back, he stood craning for four years and mocked his own pain, but the gap is the subject: God surging, Adam not yet alive, but in 1990 a doctor saw a brain in God's cloak, from an artist who dissected corpses, but for centuries no one saw these colours, so the gap belongs to Michelangelo, a repairer, a restorer and us.

script.text: Michelangelo protested he was no painter, then spent four years up there.
He didn't lie on his back: he stood, head bent back, on his own scaffold.
In a poem he mocked the pain: my beard points at heaven.
But the gap is the real subject.
God surges forward on his angels; Adam lies limp, not yet alive.
The fingers almost touch: the instant before the spark.
But in 1990, a doctor claimed something stranger: God's cloak is shaped like a human brain.
